comparison.summary: Your exact suffix structures replace the existing binary-search and rolling-hash approach, which has a confirmed collision error.
details: Your first solution builds a suffix automaton, propagates occurrence counts through the shorterId tree, and finds the shortest length represented by a node that occurs once. It takes O(n) expected time and O(n) space.

Your second solution sorts suffixes with rank doubling and stable counting sort, builds adjacent LCP values, and checks each suffix’s shortest distinguishing prefix. It takes O(n log n) time and O(n) space.
The existing Python binary-searches the length and counts rolling hashes, taking O(n log n) time and O(n) space. No JavaScript or TypeScript implementation was saved.

The existing hash-only comparison is incorrect for nums = [1,20,2,1,20,2]: it returns 3 instead of 2. With base 19, [1,20] and [2,1] both hash to 39, hiding the unique pair [2,1]. Both supplied solutions return the correct answer 2.

solutions.title: Suffix automaton
solutions.approach: Our final refactored suffix automaton: node IDs, `splitNode()`, one transition-exists check in the main loop, and occurrence propagation through the shorter-ID tree.
notes: Preserved naming: currNum, newId, lastId, shorterId, nextId, cloneId, ROOT_ID, and NO_ID. Transitions remain plain JavaScript objects.

solutions.title: Suffix array + LCP
solutions.approach: Sort suffix start indices using rank doubling and stable counting sort; calculate adjacent longest-common-prefix values (LCP); then find the shortest distinguishing prefix for each suffix. There is **no binary search** and **no automaton cloning**.
notes: Kept as a separate function so both selected implementations can remain together.
